story: Waaq (also spelled Waaq or Waaqa) is the name given to the sky God among several related peoples, including the Oromo and Somali. In the Oromo language, Waaqa still means 'God' today. The word appears in related forms among other groups: the Konso call God Waaqa, the Rendille call God Wax, the Bayso call God Wah or Waa, the Daasanach call God Waag, the Hadiyya call God Waaʔa, and the Burji call God Waacʼi. Among the Somali, God is now primarily called by an Arabic-derived name, Allaah, but the old name Waaq survives in personal and place names. The Somali clan Jidwaaq take their name from Waaq, meaning 'Path of God.' Several towns and villages in Somalia carry the name Waaq within them. The word Waaq also appears in Arabic meaning 'protector,' and is found in the Quran. Some traditions link Waaq to the Harari region. A Sufi mystic named Ibn Arabi wrote that Waaq was once a generic name for God, comparing it to the Turkic peoples' concept of Tengri. Among the Oromo and Somali, Waaq, Waaqa, or Waaqo was the name of God in a pre-Islamic monotheistic faith believed to have been held by Cushitic peoples. This belief was likely carried to the Horn of Africa by speakers of a proto-Cushitic language who migrated from North Sudan during the Neolithic era. This faith may share roots with the Religions of the Book, though it is not derived from them. The Cushites were also among the first peoples to practice circumcision, a rite central to Abrahamic religions. In recent times, use of the name Waaq has declined significantly following the arrival of Islam in the Horn of Africa.
blind: A word for the sky God appears among several related peoples in a region. In one language, the word still means 'God' today. The word appears in related forms among other groups, each with its own version of the term. Among one people, God is now primarily called by a name borrowed from a neighboring religious tradition, but the old name survives in personal and place names. A clan takes its name from the old word, meaning 'Path of God.' Several towns and villages in the region carry the old name within them. The word also appears in a neighboring language meaning 'protector,' and is found in that tradition's sacred text. Some traditions link the word to a particular region. A mystic wrote that the word was once a generic name for God, comparing it to another people's concept of a sky deity. Among these peoples, the old word was the name of God in a pre-monotheistic-religion faith believed to have been held by a broader ethnic-linguistic group. This belief was likely carried to the region by speakers of an ancestral language who migrated from a northern area during an early era. This ethnic-linguistic group was also among the first peoples to practice a bodily rite central to those other traditions.
